text: Well, I think it's also very personal to our context and our upbringing. For us, Sriram and I came from a fairly middle class family in India, this city in India that most people here won't probably know.
speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
context: Lenny asks Aarthi and Sriram about their techno-optimism movement and why it's important to them. Aarthi explains their personal background - growing up middle-class in India without easy access to computers, then eventually getting their first computers after their parents saved money. She's setting up the foundation for why technology has been so transformative in their lives and why they're advocates for tech's positive impact.
text_ko: 음, 제 생각에는 이건 우리 맥락과 성장 배경에 아주 개인적인 문제예요. 스리람과 저는 인도의 비교적 중산층 가정에서 자랐고, 우리가 자란 도시는 여기 있는 분들 대부분이 아마 모를 거예요.
text_zh: 嗯，我觉得这也挺个人化的，跟我们的背景和成长经历有很大关系。像我和Sriram，我们都是在印度一个比较中产的家庭长大的——是在印度的一个城市，很多这里的人可能都不太知道。
text_es: Bueno, creo que también depende mucho de nuestro contexto y de la crianza que tuvimos. En nuestro caso, Sriram y yo venimos de una familia más bien de clase media en la India, de una ciudad que probablemente aquí casi nadie conozca.
key_sentence: For us, Sriram and I came from a fairly middle class family in India.
original_text: Well, I think it's also very personal to our context and our upbringing. For us, Sriram and I came from a fairly middle class family in India, this city in India that most people here won't probably know. And we grew up really liking computers but didn't have access to a computer for a longest time. In both our cases, our parents bought us our first computers after saving money for it and it was a hard thing.

vocabulary.definition: The circumstances or setting surrounding an event, statement, or idea that help to clarify its meaning.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, understanding the context is crucial for making informed decisions, as it encompasses market conditions, cultural factors, and stakeholder perspectives.
vocabulary.nuance: While context is often used to provide clarity, it can also imply that certain interpretations may vary based on different situational factors.

vocabulary.definition: The treatment and education received by a child from their parents or guardians, shaping their values and behavior.
vocabulary.businessContext: In corporate environments, understanding an employee's upbringing can provide insights into their work ethic, communication style, and approach to teamwork.
vocabulary.nuance: Upbringing often carries a personal connotation, and discussing it in a professional setting may require sensitivity to avoid assumptions or stereotypes.

vocabulary.definition: A social class between the upper and working classes, typically characterized by moderate income, education, and occupation.
vocabulary.businessContext: In market analysis, the middle class is often targeted for consumer goods and services, as their purchasing power can significantly influence economic trends.
vocabulary.nuance: The term can vary by country and culture, so it is important to consider local economic conditions when discussing middle-class demographics.

text: Our first jobs were at Microsoft, we built developer tools and platforms. If you were in our shoes, you would feel the same way too. Tech has given us so much.
speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
context: Aarthi continues explaining why she and Sriram are techno-optimists. She describes their journey from India to working at Microsoft, then moving through Seattle to Silicon Valley where she started companies. She argues that technology has been transformative for their lives and careers, and expresses frustration with critics of tech because she's witnessed firsthand how technology uplifts people and creates opportunities.
text_ko: 저희 첫 직장은 마이크로소프트였고, 개발자 도구와 플랫폼을 만들었어요. 여러분이 우리 입장이었다면 같은 느낌을 받으셨을 거예요. 기술이 우리에게 정말 많은 걸 줬어요.
text_zh: 我们的第一份工作都在微软(Microsoft)，做的是给开发者用的工具和平台(developer tools and platforms)。要是你处在我们的位置，你也会有同感。科技(Tech) 给了我们很多。
text_es: Comenzamos trabajando en Microsoft; construimos herramientas y plataformas para desarrolladores (developer tools and platforms). Si estuvieras en nuestro lugar, también lo sentirías. La tecnología (tech) nos ha dado tanto.
key_sentence: Tech has given us so much.
original_text: Our first jobs were at Microsoft, we built developer tools and platforms. If you were in our shoes, you would feel the same way too. Tech has given us so much. And so for us to come here all the way from India, through multiple cities, we lived in Seattle and then here, the Bay Area, I've started tech companies, it is a bit frustrating to see the other viewpoint because you can see how much it has uplifted people, careers, lives, but also just from what we've been able to work on, what we've seen our friends work on and ship and put out there, it has dramatically moved the needle.

vocabulary.definition: Software applications or utilities that assist programmers in creating, debugging, and maintaining software applications.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the tech industry, developer tools are essential for enhancing productivity and efficiency in software development processes, often leading to faster product releases.
vocabulary.nuance: The term often implies a focus on enhancing the developer's experience and capabilities, rather than just the end product.

vocabulary.definition: Frameworks or environments that enable the development and deployment of applications, often providing a set of tools and services.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, platforms can refer to both software platforms, like operating systems, and business platforms, like marketplaces, that facilitate interactions between users and providers.
vocabulary.nuance: The term can imply a foundational role in technology ecosystems, suggesting scalability and integration capabilities.

text: you have to get out there and build your own brand... All of that is just up to you.
speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
context: Lenny asks about building personal brands and networks. Aarthi explains how she used to believe the common corporate advice to 'just put your head down and do good work' - that products would speak for themselves. However, she's come to realize this approach doesn't work in practice. She argues that professionals need to actively build their personal brand and figure out their own career direction rather than expecting companies to do it for them.
text_ko: 직접 나가서 자기만의 브랜드를 만들어야 해요. 결국 그 모든 건 당신에게 달려 있어요.
text_zh: 你得主动出去把个人品牌打造起来——这一切都得靠你自己。
text_es: Te toca salir y construir tu marca personal. Todo eso está en tus manos.
key_sentence: All of that is just up to you.
original_text: Most of my career I was like, 'Yeah, of course that makes sense, that's kind of what you do.' But I've come to realize that that is just not true and this might be a controversial opinion, but you have to get out there and build your own brand. You have to figure out what you stand for, what your core values are, what you believe in, what you think you want to do, what your next career trajectory is going to look like. All of that is just up to you.

vocabulary.definition: To create and develop a unique identity or reputation for oneself or a business in the marketplace.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, building your own brand is crucial for establishing a distinct presence that attracts customers and differentiates from competitors, especially in personal branding and entrepreneurship.
vocabulary.nuance: This phrase often implies a proactive approach to self-promotion and personal development, and is best used in contexts emphasizing individual initiative.

text: And I think building a personal brand is looked down upon so much that people think of it as a dirty word. It's like, 'No, you can't do that.' 'Oh, look at this person who's branding themselves,' kind of thing.
speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
context: Aarthi continues her response about personal branding. She addresses the negative perception many people have of personal branding, noting that it's often seen as a 'dirty word' or something unprofessional. She reframes personal branding not as boastful self-promotion, but as authentically highlighting your genuine strengths and expertise through various content channels like videos, writing, or social media.
text_ko: 저는 퍼스널 브랜딩(personal branding)을 한다는 걸 사람들이 너무 깔보거나 부정적으로 봐서, 마치 금기어처럼 여기는 것 같아요. '그건 안 돼.' '자기 브랜딩하는 사람 좀 봐.' 이런 반응이요.
text_zh: 我觉得打造个人品牌 (personal brand) 被很多人看不起，几乎成了个脏词。大家会说，“不行，你不能那样”，或者一看到有人在自我包装就开始指指点点。
text_es: Creo que construir una marca personal (personal brand) está tan mal visto que la gente lo considera una palabra sucia. Es como: "No, no puedes hacer eso." "Mira a esa persona que se está promocionando", algo así.
key_sentence: building a personal brand is looked down upon so much that people think of it as a dirty word.
original_text: And I think building a personal brand is looked down upon so much that people think of it as a dirty word. It's like, 'No, you can't do that.' 'Oh, look at this person who's branding themselves,' kind of thing. But I almost see it as what distinguishes you from everybody else and that is not so much saying something that you're not good at or touting yourself more, it's really about highlighting, 'I'm really good at this thing and I want to talk about this thing and I want to do videos about it or write about it or tweet about it.'

vocabulary.definition: A personal brand is the unique combination of skills, experiences, and personality that an individual presents to the world, particularly in a professional context.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and startup environments, a strong personal brand can enhance an individual's credibility, attract opportunities, and differentiate them from competitors.
vocabulary.nuance: While a personal brand can be empowering, it may also carry a stigma if perceived as self-promotional or inauthentic.

vocabulary.definition: Branding is the process of creating a unique identity and image for a product, service, or individual in the minds of consumers, often through the use of names, symbols, and design.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the business world, effective branding is crucial for establishing market presence, fostering customer loyalty, and differentiating offerings in competitive landscapes.
vocabulary.nuance: Branding encompasses both visual elements and the emotional connections consumers have with a brand, making it a multifaceted concept.

text: You do this, you do two coffees a week and literally just ask me two hours a week, everyone has two hours a week, it'll start compounding over overtime and time.
speaker: Sriram Krishnan
context: Sriram is giving detailed advice on how to build a professional network. He's explaining a systematic approach where you consistently meet with two people per week for coffee - just investing two hours weekly. He emphasizes how this compounds over time, and as people move to different companies over the years, you build a network of hundreds of contacts across the industry. This is part of his broader framework for authentic relationship building.
text_ko: 이렇게 해보세요. 주에 커피 두 번 정도 하면서, 말 그대로 주당 두 시간만 저한테 물어봐요. 다들 주당 두 시간은 있잖아요. 그러면 시간이 지날수록 복리 효과(compounding)처럼 쌓일 거예요.
text_zh: 你就照这么做，每周约我两次喝咖啡，真就每周花两个小时来问我问题就行。大家都能挤出每周两个小时，时间一久就会开始产生复利（compounding）效应。
text_es: Haz esto: queda para dos cafés a la semana y pídeme solo dos horas. Todos tenemos esas dos horas a la semana; con el tiempo eso se irá multiplicando.
key_sentence: Two hours a week can start compounding over overtime, expanding your network.
original_text: You do this, you do two coffees a week and literally just ask me two hours a week, everyone has two hours a week, it'll start compounding over overtime and time. And then as the years go by, you keep in touch with the people you used to work with you, these folks will go to other places, five years, six years go by, you start in your mid-20s or late 20s and you know hundreds of people all over.

vocabulary.definition: The process of accumulating interest or value over time, where the returns on an investment generate their own returns.
vocabulary.businessContext: In finance and investing, compounding is crucial as it illustrates how investments can grow exponentially over time, emphasizing the importance of starting early.
vocabulary.nuance: Compounding often carries a positive connotation, suggesting growth and increasing returns, and is typically used in discussions about long-term financial strategies.

text: The other key part is expecting nothing in return.
speaker: Sriram Krishnan
context: Sriram continues his networking advice, emphasizing the importance of authentic relationship building. He warns against transactional approaches where you're obviously seeking something (like a job), noting that people can easily detect these motives. Instead, he advocates for genuine curiosity about others and a willingness to help them. He promises that this authentic approach will build a valuable network you can eventually 'tap into' for opportunities.
text_ko: 또 다른 핵심은 보답을 기대하지 않는 거예요.
text_zh: 另一个关键是别指望有回报。
text_es: Otro punto clave es no esperar nada a cambio.
original_text: The other key part is expecting nothing in return. And generally people are very good at reading other people and if you go and being like, 'Hey, I just want to meet you because I want a job or I'm here to network,' whatever that means, they don't want to meet you. Just go and be very curious about who they are and try and help them. And you'll be surprised wherever you start, within a year, two years, you'll know hundreds of people who you can tap into, so I think that is super powerful.

vocabulary.definition: The act of giving or offering something without anticipating any compensation or reciprocation.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, this mindset can enhance goodwill and foster a positive corporate culture, as it emphasizes altruism and community engagement.
vocabulary.nuance: This phrase suggests a selfless approach to interactions, which can be beneficial in building trust but may also be misinterpreted as a lack of ambition in competitive environments.

text: That is terrible feedback and to totally ignore that... The things that work well for me and a lot of others is putting yourself out there.
speaker: Sriram Krishnan
context: Sriram is discussing personal branding and shares that both he and Aarthi have received negative feedback at work for building their personal brands too much. He strongly advises people to ignore this type of feedback, calling it 'terrible feedback.' He argues that 'putting yourself out there' through various forms of content creation and personal branding is actually beneficial for career success, contrary to what some managers might say.
text_ko: 그건 정말 형편없는 피드백이에요. 그걸 완전히 무시하다니 놀랍네요. 저와 많은 사람들에게 잘 통하는 건 자신을 적극적으로 드러내는 거예요.
text_zh: 那种反馈很糟，完全不理会不行……对我和很多人来说，有用的做法是主动把自己摆出来，争取曝光和机会。
key_sentence: Ignore terrible feedback about brand building; putting yourself out there is crucial.
original_text: Both Aarthi and I at different points in our career have gotten feedback in our job saying, 'Oh, with Sriram and Aarthi, it's brand build too much, et cetera.' I have learned that that is terrible feedback and to totally ignore that and if anybody hears anything like that, just totally ignore that. The things that work well for me and a lot of others is putting yourself out there and that can be anything.

vocabulary.definition: Information or criticism about a person's performance or behavior, often used to improve future actions.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, feedback is crucial for employee development, product improvement, and customer satisfaction, often gathered through surveys, reviews, or performance evaluations.
vocabulary.nuance: While feedback can be constructive, it may also carry negative connotations if perceived as harsh or unhelpful; thus, it is important to deliver it thoughtfully.

vocabulary.definition: The act of exposing oneself to new experiences, opportunities, or risks, particularly in social or professional contexts.
vocabulary.businessContext: In startups and business networking, putting yourself out there is vital for building connections, seeking partnerships, and promoting one's ideas or products.
vocabulary.nuance: This phrase often implies a level of vulnerability and courage, and may not be suitable in contexts where caution is warranted.

vocabulary.definition: To deliberately pay no attention to something or someone, often to dismiss or overlook it.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, ignoring feedback or market signals can lead to missed opportunities or failures, making it a critical action to avoid.
vocabulary.nuance: While ignoring can sometimes be strategic, it often carries a negative connotation, suggesting negligence or lack of awareness.

text: You'd be amazed how often somebody just have a random great Twitter thread with no followers and somebody super interesting will email them and that leads to amazing things happening, it encourages serendipity.
speaker: Sriram Krishnan
context: Sriram continues explaining the benefits of creating content and building a personal brand online. He describes how putting yourself out there acts like a 'Bat-Signal' that attracts interesting opportunities and people. He gives an example of how even someone with no followers can create great content that gets noticed by influential people, leading to unexpected opportunities. This is part of his argument for why people should ignore advice against personal branding.
text_ko: 팔로워도 거의 없는데 우연히 멋진 트위터 스레드(Twitter thread)를 올리면, 의외로 흥미로운 누군가가 메일로 연락해 와서 그게 놀라운 일들로 이어지는 경우가 정말 자주 있어요. 그런 게 뜻밖의 기회를 만들어줘요.
text_zh: 你会很惊讶：很多人几乎没粉丝，在推特(Twitter)上随手发了条很棒的推文串(thread)，结果被某个特别有意思的人发邮件联系上，进而发生很多很棒的事。这种事很容易带来意外的好机会(serendipity)。
text_es: Te sorprendería lo a menudo que alguien publica un hilo genial en Twitter (Twitter thread) sin apenas seguidores y luego alguien muy interesante le escribe por correo electrónico (email); de ahí salen cosas increíbles, fomenta la serendipia (serendipity).
key_sentence: Encourages serendipity, leading to amazing things happening from random connections.
original_text: You'd be amazed how often somebody just have a random great Twitter thread with no followers and somebody super interesting will email them and that leads to amazing things happening, it encourages serendipity. So over the years, I wish I had listened less to people who said I should not do this and listened more to the people who said I should do this more.

vocabulary.definition: The occurrence of events by chance in a happy or beneficial way.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, serendipity often refers to unexpected opportunities that arise, such as networking connections or innovative ideas that emerge from casual interactions.
vocabulary.nuance: While serendipity implies a fortunate accident, it is often used to highlight the importance of being open to new experiences and ideas.

text: Find the niche, start really small and find the niche. I think oftentimes I've seen other startup founders and I invest and advise in a lot of early stage companies.
speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
context: Lenny asks Aarthi about the key things to get right when building a new community. Aarthi, drawing from her experience building community products at Facebook and Clubhouse, plus her work as an investor and advisor to early-stage companies, emphasizes starting small and finding a specific niche. She criticizes founders who try to build massive, scaled communities from the beginning, arguing this approach sets them up for failure rather than finding focused product-market fit first.
text_ko: 틈새시장(niche)을 찾아요. 정말 작게 시작해서 그 틈새에 집중하는 게 좋아요. 제 경험상 다른 스타트업 창업자들(startup founders)을 자주 봐왔고, 저는 초기 단계 회사들(early-stage companies)에 많이 투자하고 자문해요.
text_zh: 先找准细分市场(niche)，从非常小的切入点做起，把这个细分做透。我发现很多创业者(startup founders) 往往是这么做的——我也投资并给不少早期公司(early-stage companies) 提供建议。
text_es: Encuentra un nicho: empieza muy pequeño y céntrate en ese nicho. Es algo que veo a menudo entre otros fundadores de empresas emergentes (startups); yo invierto y asesoro a muchas empresas en etapa temprana (early stage).
key_sentence: Find the niche, start really small and find the niche.
original_text: Find the niche, start really small and find the niche. I think oftentimes I've seen other startup founders and I invest and advise in a lot of early stage companies. I went through Y Combinator, so I go back to YC as much as I can and go help out folks. But oftentimes I'll see people starting companies or founders coming in and being like, 'I'm going to build this product that is going to cater to this community. I'm going to build this world's largest community off this kind of thing,' and it almost starts at this super scaled version and then they set themselves up for failure.

vocabulary.definition: A niche refers to a specialized segment of the market for a particular kind of product or service.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, identifying a niche allows companies to target specific customer needs and differentiate themselves from competitors.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'niche' often implies a smaller market, it can also suggest a unique opportunity for growth and innovation.

vocabulary.definition: A startup is a newly established business, typically in the early stages of development, focused on bringing a unique product or service to market.
vocabulary.businessContext: Startups often seek funding and mentorship to scale their operations and validate their business models in competitive environments.
vocabulary.nuance: The term 'startup' can carry a connotation of innovation and disruption, often associated with technology-driven ventures.

vocabulary.definition: Early stage refers to the initial phase of a company's development, where it is typically focused on product development, market research, and initial customer acquisition.
vocabulary.businessContext: Investors often look for early stage companies as opportunities for high growth potential, albeit with higher risk.
vocabulary.nuance: The term 'early stage' implies that the company is still refining its business model and may not yet be profitable.

vocabulary.definition: To advise means to offer recommendations or guidance to someone regarding a particular course of action.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, advising can involve providing strategic insights, mentorship, or operational guidance to startups and entrepreneurs.
vocabulary.nuance: The term 'advise' suggests a level of expertise and authority, often implying that the advisor has relevant experience or knowledge.

text: You're almost better off doing these small, niche, non-scalable things to go find these oddball set of people who are doing this, who are really interested in this one thing and kind of scale from there and grow from there.
speaker: Aarthi Ramamurthy
context: Aarthi continues her advice on community building. She advocates for deliberately doing 'non-scalable things' initially to find a core group of passionate users - what she calls an 'oddball set of people' who are deeply interested in a specific problem or topic. This is part of her broader framework that successful communities should start small and niche before attempting to scale, rather than trying to build massive communities from day one.
text_ko: 차라리 이렇게 작고 틈새 시장(niche)이고 확장 불가능한(non-scalable) 활동들을 하면서 이 한 가지에 진짜 관심 있는 독특한 사람들을 찾아가서 거기서부터 확장(scale)하고 성장해 나가는 편이 더 나아요.
text_zh: 倒不如先做一些小众、无法规模化(non-scalable) 的事，去找那群对某件事特别痴迷的人，然后从他们那里慢慢扩展、做大。
text_es: Muchas veces te conviene más hacer estas cosas pequeñas, de nicho (niche) y no escalables (non-scalable) para ir a buscar ese grupo peculiar de personas que están haciendo esto y que realmente están muy interesadas en algo concreto, y desde ahí escalar y crecer.
key_sentence: You're almost better off doing these small, niche, non-scalable things to go find these oddball set of people
original_text: You're almost better off doing these small, niche, non-scalable things to go find these oddball set of people who are doing this, who are really interested in this one thing and kind of scale from there and grow from there. And I think that's one big thing that when you're starting to build a community, don't start to build this super scaled community. Start with few people who are passionate about a particular problem and want to get together kind of thing.

vocabulary.definition: A specialized segment of the market for a particular kind of product or service.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, identifying a niche allows companies to target specific customer needs that are not being met by mainstream providers, often leading to competitive advantages.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'niche' can imply a limited audience, it often carries a positive connotation of exclusivity and specialization.

vocabulary.definition: The capability of a business or system to grow and manage increased demand without compromising performance or losing revenue potential.
vocabulary.businessContext: In startups, scalability is crucial as it indicates the potential for growth and the ability to expand operations efficiently as demand increases.
vocabulary.nuance: The term often implies not just growth, but growth that can be achieved without proportional increases in costs.
